paras: The lynching of Joe Walker was the killing of a Black man by a mob near Greenville, Florida, in March 1919, after he was taken from two police officers who were carrying him to jail at Madison. Walker had been charged with shooting a night watchman, and he was shot to death without trial. The case reached Black readers through a brief Valdosta, Georgia, dispatch and through the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People's protest to Governor Sidney J. Catts, whose reply that lynchers could not be brought to trial was printed across the Black press.

According to the dispatch, Walker was charged with shooting Nightwatchman Gerald at Greenville, Florida, on a Monday night. Chief of Police Swilley and Policeman Cooper then set out to take him to Madison, Florida, "for safe keeping." The coverage does not say whether the watchman survived.

The officers had gone "but a short distance from Greenville when the mob appeared and demanded Walker." The mob took the prisoner from them and shot him to death early in the morning. The dispatch, dated Valdosta, March 19, gave no number for the mob, named none of its members, and said nothing of resistance by the officers, attributing its account to "information received here."

No report of an inquest, arrests or a grand jury appears in the coverage. The NAACP, through its secretary John R. Shillady, wired Governor Catts on March 15 about the lynching of "two Negroes, Bud Johnson and Joe Walker," and asked that the lynchers be brought to justice. In a letter dated March 18, Catts wrote that he had not known of "the lynching at Madison" until he read of it in the papers.

Catts went on to say that trying lynchers would be impossible because "the citizenship will not stand for it," and he blamed "tramp negroes" for the violence. Shillady answered on March 28, mostly about the prisoner lynched in the Milton case, and the association made both letters public in April.

The Cleveland Advocate printed the Valdosta dispatch on March 22 under the sarcastic headline "Valdosta Scores One!", and its editorial column in the same issue mocked Valdosta as one of "Georgia's Gomorrahs," where "an American citizen" had been shot by a mob. A one-sentence version ran without comment among the Wisconsin Weekly Blade's news briefs on April 5 and was reprinted word for word by the Phoenix Tribune on May 31. The Topeka Plaindealer's editorial "Judge Lynch and the League" cited the killing as Georgia's contribution to "the era of murder," contrasting it with the "heroism of the colored soldiers" in the American Expeditionary Forces.

Walker's name was carried most widely by the Catts correspondence, which the St. Louis Argus, the Dallas Express, the Ohio State Monitor and the Chicago Defender printed in April under headlines such as "Florida Governor Defends Lynching" and "Cannot Bring Mob Leaders to Trial Says Gov." The Ohio State Monitor added an editorial charging that the governor "takes his stand with the mob." In these reports the killing itself got little detail; the papers used it mainly to condemn the governor's position.

The date is uncertain: the dispatch is dated March 19 and says the killing occurred "early today," but the NAACP's wire naming Walker is dated March 15 and Catts's reply March 18. The Cleveland Advocate's editorial gave "Wednesday, March 12" for the mob killing it placed at Valdosta.

The manner of death also differs: the dispatches say Walker was shot, while Catts quoted the NAACP as saying "the man in Madison was burned to death." The Topeka Plaindealer placed the shooting of the watchman in Jacksonville and the seizure at Valdosta, Georgia, the dispatch's dateline, rather than near Greenville.

reader.title: Lynching of Joe Walker
bases: A mob took Walker, charged with shooting a night watchman, from two officers and shot him to death (A2, A6); the NAACP and Governor Catts both spoke of it as a lynching (A10, A13).

Walker was shot to death by a 'mob' that took him from police officers while he was held on a charge of shooting a watchman (A2, A6), an extralegal killing by a group acting on a criminal accusation; the NAACP called it a lynching and the governor referred to 'the lynching at Madison' (A10).

The Valdosta dispatch (A2) and the tabloid brief (A6) agree on the core event, and separately the NAACP's wire naming Joe Walker as lynched and Governor Catts's acknowledgment of 'the lynching at Madison' (A10, A13) confirm that a lynching occurred, though the date and manner of death differ across sources.
